templates.description: The readiness gate you complete ONCE before the first recovery test is even scheduled, then keep green. Every item has a proof — if you can't point at the proof, it isn't done. This template implements all seven rows of the Phase 0 table in the testing-program article, including the three that were previously missing: recovery-region quota/capacity headroom, IaC drift, and runbook freshness.
templates.whenToUse: Complete (and keep green) before scheduling any Phase-1 recovery test. Re-verify the volatile items (replication, backups, scope) in the week before each test.
templates.name: Phase 0 — before any launch

items.text: Guardrail/SCP changes deployed and replication confirmed unbroken afterwards
items.why: Org guardrails (SCPs, permission boundaries) silently break replication tools; a policy change last Tuesday can mean zero recovery points today.
items.proof: Replication status green in the recovery tool dated AFTER the last guardrail change; change ticket linked

items.text: IaC pipeline green and the recovery-region plan is CLEAN (no drift)
items.why: A broken pipeline means rebuilding the shape by hand during the event; a dirty plan means the recovery region is not what the code says it is, and the difference will only surface at the layer that depends on it. Drift is invisible until it is a gap: anything changed in the console does not exist in git, so it will not be recreated and nobody will know it is missing.
items.proof: Link to the last successful pipeline run AND a plan/diff output for the recovery-region stack showing zero changes (or every remaining diff triaged and accepted in writing, with a ticket)

items.text: Backup/replication error count is ~0 across all protected resources
items.why: Every resource with a failing backup is a resource you will discover missing at the worst possible time.
items.proof: Recovery tool dashboard screenshot showing 0 (or triaged-and-accepted) errors

items.text: Recovery-region quota & capacity headroom confirmed for the full scale-up
items.why: Pilot light and warm standby both assume the recovery region will sell you the compute during a regional event — when every other tenant is asking for it too. Service quotas (vCPU per instance family, EIPs, NAT gateways, ENIs, ASG/spot limits) and instance-type availability are the most likely single reason a Tier-0 stack does not come back, and the tool will report a green posture right up to the InsufficientInstanceCapacity error. A scaling block asks the region; it does not reserve anything.
items.proof: Quota report vs required-at-full-scale, per quota and per instance family, dated this week — plus evidence for Tier-0 that capacity is actually held (on-demand capacity reservations) or an explicit written acceptance that it is not

items.text: Secret lists reconciled into ONE signed-off list
items.why: When the tool's replicated list, the manual spreadsheet, and the runtime logical names disagree, the disagreement is where the test dies (secrets-init crash loops).
items.proof: Single CSV of logical name → recovery ARN, signed off by app + platform leads, date on it

items.text: Known blocker secrets retrievable BY THE APPLICATION IDENTITY in the recovery region
items.why: The secrets that killed the last test are the first thing to re-check, and "we fixed it" is not evidence. Note what changed here: describe-secret is NOT evidence either — it returns metadata only (no secret value) and never exercises a KMS decrypt, so it passes when the replica is empty, when the KMS key or its policy is missing, and when the application's own role has no permission. get-secret-value forces the decrypt; running it as the workload's identity also proves the role policies and the recovery cluster's OIDC/IRSA trust made the trip.
items.proof: get-secret-value output (value redacted, exit code 0) for each previously-missing secret, executed from the tier-0 ServiceAccount/instance role in the recovery region, with the sts get-caller-identity output beside it showing the APP role

items.text: Network isolation decision confirmed: sandbox ON, with VPC endpoints in place to make it workable
items.why: The sandbox is the control that stops a drill calling real partners, emailing real customers or submitting real settlement files, so ON is the default and OFF needs a signed acknowledgement plus a verified containment check. It is workable because image pulls and secrets do not need internet egress: ECR api+dkr interface endpoints, the S3 GATEWAY endpoint (ECR layers live in S3 — this is the one people miss), Secrets Manager, regional STS, KMS and Logs interface endpoints cover it. The alternative failure mode is worse than a lost window: with egress open, a faithful copy of production does production things.
items.proof: Launch flags recorded in the test plan showing isolation ON; a list of the VPC endpoints present in the recovery VPC (ecr.api, ecr.dkr, s3 gateway, secretsmanager, sts, kms, logs); if OFF, the verbatim approver acknowledgement plus the containment probe output from inside the recovered environment

items.text: Recovery scope re-selected and saved with the vendor/tool
items.why: Scope drifts: new services appear, old ones go stale. A scope saved months ago recovers last quarter's platform.
items.proof: Scope-saved confirmation dated within a week of the test

items.text: Operator AND approver on the calendar for the full window
items.why: A test without its approver stalls at every gate; a test without a backup operator dies with one person's laptop.
items.proof: Calendar invites accepted by both, window blocked

items.text: Partner contact confirmed with a test transaction ready
items.why: The success bar is a business transaction; without the partner's test claim (or a faithful synthetic copy) you cannot prove L6.
items.proof: Message from partner engineer confirming availability + transaction payload in the repo

items.text: SSO/VPN access profiles to the recovery account tested by each operator
items.why: Discovering at T0 that nobody's credentials work in the recovery account is the most avoidable failure there is.
items.proof: Each operator has run 'aws sts get-caller-identity' against the recovery account this week

items.text: DR readiness dashboard exists and the runbook's gates can be read from it
items.why: Every 'verify' step in the runbook needs somewhere to look; grepping logs under time pressure is not a dashboard.
items.proof: Dashboard link; each runbook gate maps to a panel

items.text: Test plan written and T0 definition agreed
items.why: If T0 is not defined in advance, the RTA number will be negotiated after the fact — and nobody trusts a negotiated number.
items.proof: Test plan doc with named T0 definition, success bar, and roles

items.text: Open data-path questions answered (streams, caches, region-bound config)
items.why: Every 'does the app actually need X to answer a transaction?' left open becomes a mid-test debugging session.
items.proof: Each open question in the gap list marked answered with the answer written down

items.text: Runbook freshness: last-reviewed date is newer than the last production change it covers
items.why: A runbook older than the architecture is fiction, and it fails in the most expensive way — an operator following confident, wrong steps at 3am instead of thinking. This is the cheapest check in Phase 0 and the one most often skipped because nothing alerts on it.
items.proof: For each Tier-0 runbook: last-reviewed date vs the date of the most recent production change to the components it references (deploy log / infra PR list), plus confirmation that findings from the last test were folded in

templates.description: The short, morning-of checklist run in the first 30 minutes of the window, before anything is launched.
templates.whenToUse: Run at the start of every recovery-test or game-day window. Any red item = the decision-maker explicitly accepts it or the window is rescheduled.
templates.name: Preflight — morning of

items.text: Replication green NOW and recovery points aligned within RPO
items.why: Yesterday's green is not today's green; you launch from today's recovery points.
items.proof: Live tool dashboard check on the bridge, screenshot into the record

items.text: No active incident or in-flight deploy on the primary platform
items.why: Testing DR during a real degradation contaminates both; a mid-test deploy changes the thing you're recovering.
items.proof: Status page + deploy freeze confirmed in the platform channel

items.text: All roles present: operator, approver, partner contact reachable
items.why: Gates need the approver; the success bar needs the partner.
items.proof: Roll call on the bridge recorded

items.text: Recovery-account access verified live by today's operator
items.why: Tokens expire, roles change; test the actual hands on the actual keyboard.
items.proof: sts get-caller-identity output on the bridge

items.text: Test record open with T0 definition pasted at the top
items.why: The record is written during, not after; T0 must be written the moment it happens.
items.proof: Record doc link shared in the channel

items.text: Launch flags double-checked against the test plan
items.why: Last chance to catch wrong sandbox/isolation settings before they cost the window.
items.proof: Flags read aloud and matched to the plan

items.text: Rollback/teardown steps open in a tab and owner named
items.why: The end of the test is also a procedure; improvised teardown leaves orphaned resources billing forever.
items.proof: Named teardown owner confirms they have the steps

items.text: Time-box agreed: hard stop and bail-out criteria
items.why: Without a bail-out rule a failing test consumes the day and ends in an argument.
items.proof: Hard-stop time and bail criteria in the record

templates.description: The gate for a Phase-2 live exercise: everything that must be true before real traffic moves.
templates.whenToUse: Run at the start of a game-day window, after Phase-0 and preflight are green. Every item is a hard gate — live traffic is on the line.
templates.name: Game day — live exercise

items.text: Comms bridge open and announcement sent to all stakeholders
items.why: Live failover with surprised stakeholders becomes a political incident even when it works.
items.proof: Bridge link + sent announcement in the record

items.text: Partner engineer ON THE BRIDGE with live test transaction ready
items.why: The exercise's success bar is the partner's transaction; 'reachable by phone' is not on the bridge.
items.proof: Partner present at roll call

items.text: Decision-maker present with authority to GO, hold, and roll back
items.why: Mid-exercise decisions (extend soak? bail?) cannot wait for someone to come out of a meeting.
items.proof: Named decision-maker at roll call

items.text: Rollback rehearsed: owner states the steps from memory
items.why: The rollback is the safety net for everything else; it must be reflex, not reading.
items.proof: Verbal walkthrough on the bridge before GO

items.text: Recovery egress IPs in partner + edge allowlists (verified, not assumed)
items.why: An allowlist miss after the DNS flip means partner traffic fails publicly.
items.proof: Partner confirmation message; edge/WAF rule screenshot

items.text: A Phase-1 recovery test passed cleanly within the last quarter
items.why: Game day exercises the live edges; it must not be the first time the recovery itself is proven.
items.proof: Link to the passing test record

items.text: Maintenance window announced to customers with accurate scope
items.why: Real users may see blips during flips; honesty in advance is cheaper than apology after.
items.proof: Status-page maintenance notice live

items.text: Certificates valid on the recovery edge for the public domain
items.why: A cert mismatch turns the flip into an instant, very visible outage.
items.proof: openssl s_client check output pre-flip

items.text: DNS TTLs lowered ahead of the window
items.why: A 3600s TTL makes both the flip and the rollback glacial; lower it a day before.
items.proof: dig showing current TTL at the reduced value

items.text: Soak duration and patience window agreed before GO
items.why: 'How long do we wait before rolling back?' must be answered while everyone is calm.
items.proof: Numbers written in the record before the flip

items.text: Monitoring dashboards for BOTH regions open on the bridge
items.why: You need to see traffic decay in one region and rise in the other to know the flip worked.
items.proof: Dashboard links pinned in the bridge channel

items.text: Decision log open; scribe assigned
items.why: Game days generate decisions at speed; unrecorded decisions get re-litigated for months.
items.proof: Scribe named at roll call; log doc linked

templates.description: The short weekly loop that keeps readiness from silently rotting between tests.
templates.whenToUse: Run (and reset) every week, ideally in a standing 15-minute slot. Trend the failures — a hygiene item red two weeks running is a gap.
templates.name: Weekly DR hygiene

items.text: Replication/backup errors reviewed and at ~0
items.why: Errors accumulate silently; weekly triage keeps the recovery-point promise real.
items.proof: Tool dashboard checked; new errors ticketed

items.text: New/changed infrastructure reviewed for recovery-scope inclusion
items.why: Anything shipped this week that isn't in scope is a future missing dependency.
items.proof: This week's infra PRs cross-checked against the scope list

items.text: Secrets added/rotated this week reflected in the signed-off list
items.why: The reconciled secret list decays one rotation at a time.
items.proof: Diff of the secret list reviewed

items.text: Open DR gaps reviewed: severities current, one item moved forward
items.why: A gap list nobody burns down is a risk register in costume.
items.proof: Gap board updated; at least one status change

items.text: Next test/game-day date still on the calendar with roles confirmed
items.why: Test dates slip by default; confirming weekly makes slipping a decision instead of an accident.
items.proof: Calendar checked; attendees still accepted

items.text: DR dashboard reviewed for stale panels or broken queries
items.why: A dashboard that rotted is worse than none — it answers gates with lies.
items.proof: Each panel loads with current data
